paragraphs.text: [BOOK ONE.]

In the preceding work we set out, as well as our capacity allowed, what the Lord poured into us and what our understanding discovered concerning paradise, and in it the fall of Adam and Eve was covered. Now, since that guilt did not stay with those who began it but, what is worse, found an heir worse than they, let us take up the story that follows and pursue in our work what is joined to it according to the divine Scriptures.

Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, and said: I have acquired a man through God. When we acquire things, it is usual to consider from what, by whom and through what we acquire them: from what, as from the material; by whom, meaning who is the author; through what, as through some instrument. Does she then say, "I have acquired a man through God," so that you should take God to be an instrument? Certainly not, but so that you should understand God as the author and worker. So she ascribed more to God by saying, "I have acquired a man through God": so too, when we acquire anything, and indeed in all good fortune, we ought to ascribe it to God rather than claim it for ourselves. And in addition she bore Abel.

When something is added, what was there before is taken away. This can be gathered from the proportions of arithmetic or from the thoughts of the mind. When a number is added, a different number results and the former one is done away with, and a new thought coming in shuts out the one before it. So when Abel is added, Cain is removed. This is grasped more fully from the meaning of the names. Cain was called "acquisition," because he acquired everything for himself. Abel was one who referred everything to God, devoted to him with the pious attention of his mind. Unlike his elder brother he claimed nothing for himself, but gave the Creator credit for everything he had received from him.

So there are two schools of thought, under the names of two brothers, fighting each other and opposed to each other. One credits everything to its own mind, as though the mind were the ruling principle and, as it were, the author of all thought, sensation and movement. That is, it attributes every discovery to human ingenuity. The other ascribes everything to God as the worker and creator of all things, and submits all things to his governance as parent and ruler. The first is signified by Cain, the second is called Abel. One soul gives birth to these two schools, and so they are regarded as siblings, because they take their origin in one womb. But they are opposites, because once they have been brought forth by a kind of birth of the soul they must be divided and separated, for those at war cannot share one lodging forever. So it was with Rebecca. She was in labor with two natures of the human disposition, one evil and the other good, and felt them leaping within her womb, for Esau was a type of wickedness and Jacob bore the figure of goodness. She wondered why she perceived a kind of discord in the offspring she had conceived, and consulted God, asking him to reveal the affliction and give a remedy. To her prayer this answer was given: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall come forth from your belly. If you apply this to the soul, you will understand that the soul is the mother of both good and evil, because both flow from the one source of the soul. But sober judgment rejects the evil and, as it were, nourishes and strengthens what is good. So before the soul gives birth to the good, that is, to the reverence owed to God by which it ascribes everything to him, it puts its own interests first. But when it has brought forth the confession that is offered to God, it lays aside the swollen pride of its heart. So God, by adding to the soul the good teaching, Abel, took away the wicked teaching, Cain.

Yet in this passage I understand, in keeping with Scripture, rather the mystery of two peoples. By adding to his Church the faith of the devout people, God took away the faithlessness of the people who transgressed. The very words seem to mean this, when God says: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall come forth from your belly. This figure of the synagogue and the Church was foreshadowed long before in these two brothers, Cain and Abel. Cain stands for the parricidal people of the Jews, who hunted down the blood of their Lord and Maker, who by his birth from the Virgin Mary was also their brother, so to speak. Abel stands for the Christian who clings to God, as David also says: But for me it is good to cling to God. David said this so as to join himself to heavenly things and separate himself from earthly ones. And elsewhere he says: My soul has fainted for your word, because he had placed the ordering and practice of his life not in earthly pleasures but in knowledge of the Word. From this we see that what we read in the books of Kingdoms was not written idly but with careful weighing and examination: And he was gathered to his fathers. We are meant to understand that he was like his fathers in faith. So it is clear that he was gathered not into the burial of the body but into the fellowship of life.

Likewise it is thought that it was not written carelessly of Isaac that, leaving behind the form of this body that was joined to his soul, he was gathered to his kind, because he held fast to the ways of his father. And it is fitting that Scripture says "to his kind," not "to his people," as elsewhere. In other places we read that men were gathered to their people, but those were not so outstanding. More outstanding is the man who was like the few and not the many, since a man's people is larger than his kind, and it is counted more outstanding to be like the few than like the many. This man was begotten by God's promise and chosen for the sacrifice that tested his piety. He was content with one wife, that is, with the companionship of wisdom alone. So divine Scripture had to testify that he was an imitator of that heavenly kind which is one and always consistent with itself, not of common baseness. Where there is labor, instruction and practice, there is a college shared with many and a sort of popular fellowship, for most people make progress by listening, and these Scripture has called a people. But where learning is grasped not by human tradition but by natural insight, without toil, there is the unspoiled purity of a lofty kind. And so we read that Isaac, as a gift of God, was gathered to his kind rather than to his people, so that you may recognize that he was a diligent imitator of things divine rather than human.

Blessed too is the mind that rises above species and even above kind itself, and deserves to hear what was said to Moses when he was being set apart from the people: But you, stand here with me. In Isaac the type of the Lord's incarnation surpassed the custom of human generation and outdid those before him, so that what excelled in him was no common, popular grace but a special privilege. As the reading teaches: The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed," which is Christ. So also in Moses the figure of the teacher who was to come went beyond the dignity of the human condition, so far that he was granted the name of God. That teacher would teach the law, preach the gospel, fulfill the old testament, establish the new, and give heavenly food to the peoples. As we find it written, the Lord says: I have made you a god to Pharaoh. He was victor over all passions, and no enticements of the world could capture him. He had covered all this bodily dwelling with the purity of a heavenly way of life, ruling the mind, subduing the flesh and disciplining it with a kind of royal authority. So he was called by the name of God, to whose likeness he had shaped himself through the richness of perfect virtue.

That is why we do not read of him, as of the others, that he failed and died. We read that he died through the word of God, for God suffers neither failing nor diminishing, nor does he admit of addition. So Scripture also added that no one knows his burial place to this very day, so that you may understand that he was taken up rather than destroyed, for death is a kind of separation of soul and body. He died, then, through the word of God, as Scripture says, not according to the word. Notice that what is expressed is not a report of death but a gift of grace. He was taken up rather than left behind, and no one knows his burial place. Who on earth could find the remains of a man whom the Son of God showed in the gospel to be with him? Indeed Elijah too was seen together with him. Elijah was taken up in a chariot, and we do not read that he was buried or died, for he who is with the Son of God lives. Moses, on the other hand, we do read died, but he died through the word of God, through which all things were made. And by the word of God the heavens were established, so through the word of God there is no collapse of the work but its firm foundation. So he is not found as one who fell back into the earth when his body was dissolved, but as one endowed by the working and gift of the heavenly Word, so that his flesh received rest rather than a tomb.

The distinction between master and servant is rightly kept, so that you may understand the prerogative of the Master and the grace of the servant. Of Moses we read that no one knows his burial place, but of Christ that his burial was taken up from the earth. Moses, according to the mystery of the law, awaited redemption so that he might rise again. Christ, according to the gift of the gospel, did not await redemption but bestowed it. So his burial was not unknown but raised up. Creation could not hold it for long, because through him all creation hastened to be raised up from the bondage of corruption. No one, then, knows the burial place of Moses, because everyone has known his life. But we have seen the burial place of Christ, and yet now we no longer know it, because we have come to know his resurrection. His tomb had to be known so that his resurrection might be made manifest. That is why the gospel describes the tomb in the fullest detail, while the law does not look for it. Although the law announced his resurrection, the narrative of the gospel has proved it to us most fully.

So, to finish what we set out to do: in addition, it says, she bore Abel. That is, Eve, who had sinned grievously before, brought forth from herself a better conviction, so as to cancel the error of the earlier one. Call me a liar if this is not proved in everyone. We are born in such a way that first there is in us the weak understanding of infancy, and afterward that of childhood, which knows only the care of the body and has no worship and no observance of divine things. That is why the prophet, to prove that Jesus Christ was born of a virgin with a manifest newness of nature, says: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel. Butter and honey he shall eat before he knows evil or good; for before he knows good or evil he does not trust in wickedness, so as to choose what is good. And further on: Before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he shall receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. He alone was not captured by the vanity of this world and the swelling pride of the flesh, since he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. He is far unlike each of us, who exalt ourselves in vain, puffed up by the mind of the flesh. So no one is without sin, not even an infant one day old, but he committed no sin. And so in us Cain, who puts himself first, is born first, and afterward Abel is begotten, in whom there is reverence for God. First, then, what is evil creeps in, and afterward what is good is recognized. But where there is good, there is justice, and where there is justice, there is holiness. That is Abel, who clings to God.

And Abel, it says, became a shepherd of sheep, but Cain worked the land. It is not without purpose that Abel is put first in this place, although Cain was born first, as the reading teaches, so that the order of the names is not the order of nature. What does this change of order mean, that the younger is mentioned first where their way of life and their work are described? Let us inquire into the difference between their occupations, to find the reason for the preference. Working the land comes first in practice, but it ranks below pasturing sheep in favor, for pasturing sheep is like the work of a teacher and ruler. So it was fitting that the elder began from the older occupation, while the younger put first the newer one, which would sprout no thorns or thistles and was subject to no sentence. Indeed Adam, guilty of sin, was sent out of the paradise of delight to work the land. Rightly, then, where these brothers are born, the order of nature is also kept in naming them. But where the discipline of life is set out, the younger is placed before the elder, because although he is younger in time he is superior in virtue. Innocence is later in time than wickedness and nearly of an age with it, but it is older in the nobility of its merits. Old age is venerable not when white with years but in character. And, it says, a spotless life is the true age of old age. So where birth is described, let Cain come first, and where disciplines are set forth, let Abel run ahead. Who would deny, then, that adolescence and the first years of youth seethe with the enticements of various passions? And who would deny that when a more mature age has followed, the storm of budding wantonness is dispelled, calm is restored, and the soul's weary vessel is drawn up into quiet harbors? So the violent impulses of our youth are calmed in the safe anchorage of old age.

Taught by such examples from nature, then, do not doubt that wickedness comes first in time but remains a youngster in weakness. Wickedness has the wage of age, but virtue has the prerogative of glory, which the unjust man usually yields to the just before the judge. Faithful divine Scripture is witness to this. It teaches that Esau, a man named for folly, patiently yielded his birthright to his brother Jacob, so that he said: What good is the birthright to me? But what Esau held cheap, the man named for exercise sought to earn. Does it not seem to you that Esau was like a man beaten in a contest? He judged himself no match because of the weakness of his own mind, and yielded the crown to the victor, whom he saw bent by no enticements of the passions, though he himself could not bear even their dust. What good, he says, is the birthright to me? Among the slothful there are no badges of virtue, but among the wise they are held in the highest regard, for the pursuits of virtue are a kind of instrument. Just as a warrior cannot be without weapons, so virtue cannot be without exercise. That is why the Lord says in the gospel: From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven is taken by force, and those who use force seize it. And elsewhere: Seek the kingdom of God, and behold, all things are ready for you. Rewards are promised not to those who sleep or idle, but to those who keep watch and toil, [?] but a wage is prepared for toil. Toil may not be pleasant or attractive, but it is fruitful in reward. The word of the law teaches this, as we find it written:

If a man, it says, has two wives, one loved and the other hated, and both of them, the loved and the hated, bear him sons, and the firstborn son belongs to the hated wife, then on the day he leaves his sons as heirs of his property he may not give the birthright to the son of the loved wife, passing over the son of the hated one. He shall acknowledge the firstborn son of that wife and give him a portion of all that he has, because he is the first of his sons and the firstfruits are owed to him. What profound secret mysteries lie hidden in the letter! Recognize your offspring, O soul, and seek the mystery of this hated woman. You will find it within you, if you look for it. Go back over your thoughts and review your feelings, and you will recognize to whom the firstfruits are owed. Two women live with each of us. They are at odds in enmity and discord, and fill the house of our soul with something like jealous quarrels. One of them is sweet and dear to us, a coaxing counselor of charm, and she is called Pleasure. We think of her as our companion and part of our household. The other we believe to be harsh, rough and savage, and her name is Virtue.

Pleasure, then, is brazen in her harlot's movements, and her walk is loose from soft living. With roving eyes and playful eyelids she casts nets in which she catches the precious souls of young men, for the eye of a harlot is a snare for the sinner. Whenever she sees a man of wavering mind passing by at the corner of her house, she accosts him with charming words and makes the hearts of young men flutter. She is restless at home and wanders in the streets, lavish with kisses, cheap in modesty, rich in dress, her cheeks painted. Since she cannot have the true beauty of nature, she peddles with counterfeit cosmetics the appearance of affected beauty, not its reality. Girded with a retinue of vices and surrounded by a sort of chorus of wickedness, this leader of crimes attacks the wall of the human mind with siege engines of words like these: I have a peace offering; today I pay my vows. That is why I came out to meet you, longing to see your face, and I have found you. I have woven my bed with bands and spread it with coverings from Egypt. I have sprinkled my bed with saffron and my house with cinnamon. Come, let us enjoy friendship until dawn; come, let us wrestle in desire. Through the mouth of Solomon we see the figure of the harlot portrayed in this way. For what is so like a harlot as worldly pleasure? She enters at the window of her house, rehearsing her first temptations on the eyes, and quickly gets in if you look out into the street, that is, onto the public roads of passersby, instead of fixing the gaze of your mind on the inner mysteries of the law. It is surely she who, with stronger bonds, weaves a sort of couch out of the companionship we share with her, so that whoever reclines on it is bound. With a veil of shameful deceit she covers the bed of her body to entice the souls of young men, concealing the absence of her husband, that is, neglect of the law. For the law is absent for those who sin; if it were present, there would be no wrongdoing. And so she says: For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a very long journey, taking a bag of money in his hand. What am I to say this means, unless perhaps that the rich think there is nothing that does not yield to their money, and want the law to be for sale to suit them? Pleasure scatters her perfumes because she does not have the fragrance of Christ. She displays treasures, promises kingdoms, pledges unending love, promises untried couplings, learning without a tutor, conversation without a monitor, life without care, soft sleep, insatiable desire. Leading him astray, it says, with much flattery of words, and binding him with the snares of her lips, she drew him all the way home. And he followed her, entrapped. The hall shone, splendid with royal luxury and carved walls, and the floors swam with wine on the wet ground. The ground was fragrant with ointment, covered with fish bones and slippery with flowers already wilting. There was the uproar of revelers, the shouting of rivals, the blows of brawlers, the harmony of singers, the din of dancers, the guffaws of laughers, the applause of the wanton. Everything was confused, nothing was in nature's order. There were dancing girls with cropped hair and boys with curled locks, the indigestion of the banqueters, the belching of the eaters, the thirst of the drunkards, yesterday's hangover and today's intoxication. The cups were full of the drinkers' vomit and gave off a stronger smell of drunkenness than if they reeked only of fresh wine. Standing in the middle, she herself says: "Drink and get drunk, so that each of you may fall and not rise again. First with me is the man who is most abandoned of all. He is mine who is not his own. He is dearer to me who is worse to himself. The golden cup of Babylon is in my hand, making all the earth drunk; all nations have drunk of my wine. Let whoever is most foolish turn aside to me, and to those who lack wisdom I give this instruction: Enjoy hidden bread with pleasure, and drink stolen water, which is sweeter. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. Our life will pass like the traces of a cloud and be scattered like a mist. Come, then, let us enjoy the good things that exist and make use of creation swiftly, as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of the season pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither. Let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through; everywhere let us leave signs of our merriment. Here everything is left behind, and no one will take anything with him except what he has enjoyed through bodily pleasure. Indeed, I myself founded philosophy. And there is no truer philosophy than the one which asserts that the good is what is sweet and pleasant. So believe either philosophy or the wisdom of Solomon."

Hearing these words, he stands stuck fast, wounded like a stag shot through the liver with an arrow. Virtue pities him, and seeing that he will soon fall, she suddenly runs to meet him, fearing that if there is delay the human mind may be captured by soothing enticements. "I have appeared to you openly," she says, "though you were not looking for me, so that the unbridled and luxurious woman who knows no shame may not deceive you in your folly and entrap you. She sits at the doors of her house on a seat, openly in the streets, calling to those who pass by. Now, therefore, my son, listen to me and attend to the words of my mouth. Let not your heart turn aside into her ways, for she has wounded and cast down many, and those she has slain are countless. Her house is the way to the underworld, leading down to the chambers of death. So put a crooked mouth away from you, and drive unjust lips far from you. Let your eyes look straight ahead, and pay no heed to a deceitful woman. Honey drips from the lips of a harlot, and for a time it makes your throat rich, but afterward you will find it more bitter than gall. The day would fail me before I could list her vices, but they are described and portrayed by the mouth of Wisdom in Proverbs. Do not let desire for beauty overcome you. Her beauty is counterfeit and smeared with cosmetics, and it by no means shines with true and genuine loveliness. Do not be captured by her eyes, for nets are spread all around. Be rather like him, and follow him who leaps upon the mountains and bounds over the hills, looking through the windows, rising above the nets. The bonds of pleasure are evil. She delights the eyes and soothes the ears, but she defiles the mind. She tells many lies, adds falsehoods, takes away truths. She pledges money and offers gold, but she takes away discipline. But you, take discipline rather than money, and knowledge above tested gold, for it is better than precious stones. I will not hide from you what are said to be her greatest offers, so that I may not seem to expose what is displeasing in pleasure while keeping in the shadow what is pleasing. She lifts up and exalts the mind with persuasive words and shows it all the kingdoms of the earth, saying: All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me. There, beware of being captured by things that slip past and do not last, for in them lies a great temptation."

The Lord Jesus has certainly taught you how to resist temptations of this kind. The devil had first set the snare of gluttony, saying: "If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread." The Lord answered: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." With this saying he undid the snare. Again the devil laid a second snare, that of boastfulness, which often strangles even a good mind running along prosperous paths. "And he led him," it says, "to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here; for it is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you to guard you, for they will bear you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone." And so, although the Lord Jesus could have thrown himself down without any danger, since spiritual flight was at his disposal, yet so that there should be no kind of boastfulness, he answered the devil: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." At the same time he taught us to beware of doing the devil's will. If, then, boasting even of what is true must be avoided, how much more ought no one to boast of falsehoods as though they were true? There remains the third snare, that of avarice and ambition. Having placed him on a mountain, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. Well is it said "in a moment," for they cannot last long. Wait a little, and they quickly pass away. So those who pursue them seem to themselves to be on a mountain, but they do not last, as you have it written: "I saw the wicked man exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not." But whoever sets the highest value on these things seems to worship the devil, whose god is his belly and whose glory is in his shame. But you, seek your glory in God, who says to you: "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone" — from him you may receive eternal things, not temporal ones.

Yet if these things too delight anyone, let them be sought with more moderation from him who is the true source of all things. For even those very possessions which the devil seems to own as his own belong to another, as he himself said: "To you I will give all this power and their glory, for they have been handed over to me." Hope, then, from him — though for a short life no long provision for the journey should be sought — yet hope from him who founded the whole creation, who handed these things over to the devil for a time, not that he might possess them, but that he might tempt; for there could be no crown without a contest. The doubtful had to be tested, so that the just might be crowned.

So he gave these things to the devil, because in these very things lies the punishment of the one who receives them, if he does not know how to use them. For what is treasure to the self-indulgent man but the means of indulgence? But it is not the self-indulgent man who is approved, but the frugal. And therefore use what is set before you as a frugal man, so that you do not become hateful by eating much; for "sleeplessness and torments are for the gluttonous man," and further on: "If you have been forced to eat, get up and vomit, and it will refresh you, and you will not bring sickness on your body." So gluttony has killed very many, frugality none; wine has harmed countless people, thrift no one. Many have breathed out their souls at banquets and filled the tables with their own blood. In others indigestion has snatched away voice and senses together; and if indigestion did no harm to some, drunkenness brought them to ruin. Drunkenness has driven some into crime, though it is itself a crime; others it has reduced to poverty. Finally, hear whom Christ shuts out. "When the master of the house," he says, "has come in and shut the door, you will begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying: Open to us. And he will answer and say: I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity. Then you will begin to say: We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets. And he will say to you: I do not know where you are from." You have heard what he said about those who eat; hear now what he says about those who fast: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst now, for they shall be filled," and further on: "Woe to you

who are full, for you shall hunger." But do you want to eat, do you want to drink? Come to the banquet of Wisdom, who invites everyone with a great proclamation, saying: "Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you." Do songs delight you, to soothe you as you feast? Hear her exhorting you. Hear the Church singing, not only in songs but also in the Song of Songs: "Eat, my neighbors, and drink, and be drunk, my brothers." But this drunkenness makes men sober; this is a drunkenness of grace, not of intoxication. It brings forth gladness, not staggering. Nor need you fear that at the Church's banquet you will lack pleasant fragrances, or sweet foods, or a variety of drinks, or noble guests, or seemly servants. What is nobler than Christ, who at the Church's banquet both serves and is served? Attach yourself to the side of this guest as he reclines, and join yourself to God; do not disdain the table which Christ has chosen, saying: "I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices, I have eaten my bread with my honey, and I have drunk my wine with my milk." In the garden — that is, in paradise — is the Church's banquet, where Adam was before he committed sin. There Eve reclined, before she conceived and brought forth guilt. There you will gather myrrh, that is, the burial of Christ, so that, buried with him through baptism into death, you too may rise again just as he rose from the dead. There you will eat the bread that strengthens the heart of man; you will taste the honey that makes the passages of your throat sweet. You will drink wine with milk, that is, with brightness and purity — whether because it is pure simplicity, or because it is the spotless grace received for the forgiveness of sins, or because it nurses the little ones at the breasts of its consolation, so that, once weaned, they may grow up amid delights to the fullness of mature age. Come forward, then, to this banquet. Or are you afraid that the house may be too narrow and the banqueting place too small, and crowd you? "O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of his possession! It is great and has no end, lofty and immeasurable. There were those giants who were from the beginning, of great stature, skilled in war. These God did not choose." And rightly he did not choose them, because they knew war, not peace; and therefore you must learn peace, so that you may be chosen by God. But lest you perhaps think the great house unadorned, and you take pleasure in colonnaded lodgings: "Wisdom has built herself a house and set up seven pillars." The Lord Jesus himself also mentions that there are many dwelling places with his Father. In this house, then, you will feast on food for the soul and drink for the mind, so that afterward you may never hunger or thirst; for whoever eats there eats until he is satisfied, and whoever drinks drinks until he is drunk.

But this drunkenness is the guardian of chastity, while that drunkenness of wine is the kindling of lust, by which the inner organs are heated through the flesh, the mind catches fire, and the soul is burned up. Lust is a savage goad to crimes, which never allows the affections to remain at rest. By night it seethes, by day it pants; it rouses from sleep, draws away from business, calls back from reason, takes away good judgment; it disquiets lovers, bows down the fallen, lies in wait for the chaste; it is inflamed by possession and kindled by use. There is no limit to sinning, and the insatiable thirst for wickedness cannot be quenched except by the death of the lover. And so the apostle says: "Flee fornication," so that by swift flight we may escape the cruelty of a mistress, as of a raging one, and get free of a hideous slavery.

What shall I say of avarice, that insatiable desire for money and a kind of lust for bronze, which the more it has seized, the more it believes itself to be in want? Envious of all, cheap to itself, needy amid the greatest riches, in its feelings it shrinks what it has in abundance in its estate. There is no limit to plundering where there is no measure to desiring. It so inflames the mind, so feeds the mind with its own fire, that it differs from lust in this alone: that the one is an adulteress of beautiful bodies, the other of lands. It shakes the elements: it furrows the sea, digs up the earth, wearies heaven with prayers; pleased neither by fair weather nor by cloud, it condemns the yearly harvests and finds fault with the produce of the lands. But this is a sickness of the soul, not health. Accordingly Ecclesiastes says: "There is an evil sickness which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the harm of the one who possesses them," and above: "He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver. Nor is there an end to their acquiring." If you seek treasures, take the invisible and hidden ones, which you are to seek in the heights of heaven, not in the veins of the earth. Be poor in spirit, and you will be rich, whatever your estate, because a man's life does not consist in an abundance of riches, but in virtue and faith. These riches will make you truly rich, if you are rich toward God.'

You have heard the mysteries of pleasure; you have heard also the gifts of our own wealth, which I thought should not be covered over with ornate furnishings but displayed in the bare words of Scripture, so that they might shine with their own light and of themselves speak out for one another. For the sun and moon need no interpreter; they have as their interpreter the brightness of their own light, with which the whole world is filled. Their illumination is their proof — a witness, so to speak, that needs no summons and no informant, that requires no outside testimony and suddenly pours itself out before the eyes of all. So our works are not announced; they cry out and announce themselves. To be sure — so that I do not pass over this either, which is thought laborious in what we teach — faith is required, zeal is desired, deeds are sought. For by these three the Lord Jesus defined the duties of human devotion, saying: "Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you," and further on: "Everyone, then, who hears these words of mine and does them is like a wise man."

Whoever has zealously pursued these will receive the primacy of blessing, like the patriarch Jacob, who by self-control and faith supplanted the footsteps of human passions. He says: "God has had mercy on me, and I have all things." Let us, then, merit this mercy by faith, zeal and works, the disciplines by which Israel found the grace of God and through it all things; for he rejoiced that he had at his disposal not the riches of this world, but the disciplines of the virtues. Let us appoint these as our heirs, just as holy Abraham appointed them for himself in his son Isaac, assigning the whole inheritance of his works to a wise and just man and leaving no right of inheritance to the maidservants or the maidservants' sons, but only gifts. For perfect virtues receive the whole patrimony of glory, while some trifle is sprinkled on the ordinary and middling ones. And so Hagar, whose name in Latin means stranger and sojourner, and Keturah, whose name means fragrant, are not heirs. For whoever practices the middling disciplines is a sojourner in wisdom, not an inhabitant. Sprinkled with fragrance, he is not filled with fruit. It is food, not fragrance, that brings health, for fragrance is only the herald of fruit. So we recognize that for those who follow them the principal disciplines are to be preferred, as the native-born are to sojourners. This is according to the natural sense.

But according to the mystery, Abraham, the father of the nations, handed down the whole inheritance of his faith to his lawful seed, which is Christ — Abraham, who was like a stranger in this land, so that he carried away the fragrance of this life rather than its fruit. When the mind hears these things, it turns away from pleasure and joins itself to virtue, admiring the grace of true beauty: her pure affection, her simple judgment, her modest dress — that is, "not in persuasive speech but in the demonstration of the Spirit," which is the form of the apostolic teaching — resplendent in a cloak of wisdom and piety more precious than any gold, and accompanied by the choir of prudence, temperance, fortitude and justice, which breathe out the fragrance of the disciplines, striking reverence and pouring in grace. So, moved by such things, the mind chooses the pursuits of virtue, to which Jacob, a man full of exercise, applied his mind. And therefore he is presented as a shepherd of sheep, because to command the body and its senses and pleasures, and to keep measure in speech so that it does not wander astray like a sheep, is judged more excellent than ruling peoples and governing cities; for it is harder for anyone to rule himself than another. To conquer one's spirit, to restrain anger, and to bring the warring laws of flesh and mind into unity is the mark of a man who is in a sense immortal, whom the gate of hell could not hold. Accordingly the lawgiver himself claimed this task for himself, to pasture the sheep of Jethro, whose name means superfluous, and to drive them into the desert, because he constrained the irrational loquacity of superfluous and vulgar speech into certain secret mysteries of sober teaching. And therefore shepherds of sheep were an abomination to the Egyptians; for all who are given over to the passions of the body and indulge such pleasures of theirs shun with a kind of loathing the one who examines the word and teaches virtue. And therefore through these riddles Moses taught that the sacrifices fit for God are those which every fool flees, that is, the works and precepts of virtue. And therefore we read that Abel was a shepherd, but Cain a tiller of the earth, who, being a foolish man, could not bear the form and image of virtue displayed in his brother.

"And it happened after some days that Cain offered a gift to the Lord from the fruits of the earth." A double fault: first, that he offered after some days; second, that he offered from the fruits, not from the firstfruits. A sacrifice, however, is commended both by promptness and by graciousness. Hence the command: "If you make a vow, do not delay to pay it; for it is better not to vow a vow than to vow and not pay." For when you delay, you do not pay. Now a vow is a request for good things from God with a promise to render a gift in return. And therefore, when you have obtained what you asked for, it is ungrateful to be slow with what you promised. But sometimes either forgetfulness of what was obtained creeps over the careless, or the swollen and proud like to claim the outcome for themselves and ascribe it to their own virtues, not attributing it to the grace of its author but regarding themselves as the authors of their own goods. A third kind is a lesser sin, to be sure, but an arrogance nearly as great: that of those who do not deny that God is the giver of good things, but think that whatever has befallen them was rightly conferred on them on account of their prudence and the merits of their other virtues; and that they were held worthy of divine grace precisely because they seemed by no means unworthy that such things should come to them through God's benefits.

So that nothing of this kind may happen, whereby your vow becomes a sin for you, the law has formed and instructed you, the Lord who gave the law saying: "Take heed to yourself, lest you forget the benefits of the Lord your God and do not keep his commandments and judgments and ordinances, which I command you today; lest, when you have eaten and been filled, and have built fine houses and begun to live in them, and when your sheep and your oxen have multiplied, and you are full of bronze, silver and gold, and have begun to possess all things, and your barns are full, you exalt your heart and forget the Lord your God." You will forget the Lord, then, when you have forgotten yourself. But if you recognize that you are weak, you will recognize that God is above all things, and you cannot be unmindful of paying him the reverence you owe.

Learn now how each person is warned not to think himself the author of his own goods. "Do not say in your heart," it says, "My strength and my power have gained me this great strength; but you shall keep the Lord your God in mind, because it is he who gives you power to gain strength." Hence the apostle, as an interpreter of the law, rightly did not glory in his own strength, but said that he was the least of the apostles, and that whatever he was belonged to divine grace and not to his own merit, and that we have nothing which we have not received. "For what do you have," he says, "that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?" You have learned, then, to follow humility rather than arrogance, to aim at diligence rather than power. You have received saving precepts; do not neglect the useful instruments of medicine, by which every fiber of a deadly wound is cut away.

Let him also who justifies himself not be puffed up with the swelling of his heart; he too has received a wholesome command, the oracle resounding to this effect: "Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God begins to destroy those nations before you: Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to possess this land; but it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord will root them out before you. Not because of your righteousness, nor because of the uprightness of your heart have you entered to possess this land, but because of the wickedness of the nations the Lord will destroy them from before you, and he will establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers." This covenant, or testament, is the perfect grace of God; for God gives nothing imperfect, and virtue and the works of virtue are perfect. Now a testament is that by which an inheritance of goods is conveyed. Rightly is it called both a testament and divine, since the things that are truly good are conferred with the attestation of heavenly commands. And it is called a testament because it was dedicated with blood, the old in figure, the new in truth. By this testament we hold the pledge of divine grace, for God so loved this world that he gave his only Son for us all. Hence the apostle, proclaiming the perfection of grace, says: "How has he not also given us all things with him?"

The first grace of a vow, then, is promptness in paying it. Accordingly Abraham, when he was ordered to offer his son as a burnt offering, did not offer him after some days, as Cain did, but "rising early he saddled his donkey and took with him two servants and Isaac his son, and having cut the wood for the burnt offering he rose and went, and came on the third day to the place which God had told him." First note the ready and hastening zeal of the man about to sacrifice, so that there was no delay of waiting except until the oracle had been heard; then that he saddled his donkey himself, took all the service upon himself and prepared what was needed for the sacrifice, and led his victim accompanied, as it were, by the two virtues of faith: certain of God's power and secure in his goodness.

As for the words "on the third day": either they mean that devotion ought to be continuous and perpetual — for time is threefold, past, present and future, and by this we are reminded that no forgetfulness of God's benefits, whether past, present or future, ought to creep in, but a tenacious memory of his grace should persist and obedience should never fail — or they mean that whoever sacrifices ought to believe in the one splendor, the one light of the Trinity; for to him who sacrifices faithfully it is always day, and there is no night. So also in Exodus Moses says: "We will go a three days' journey and sacrifice to the Lord our God." And elsewhere too, when God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre, "Abraham," it says, "looked up with his eyes and saw, and behold, three men stood over him. And seeing them he ran to meet them at the door of his tent and bowed down to the ground and said: Lord, if I have found favor before you." He sees three, he worships one; he offers three measures of fine flour. For though God is beyond measure, yet he holds the measure of all things, as it is written: "Who has measured the water in his hand and the heavens with his palm and the whole earth in his closed hand?" So the holy patriarch offered to the Trinity, perfect in each of its persons, a sacrifice in the inner recesses of his mind, that is, a sacrifice of spiritual fine flour. This is the fine flour which in the Gospel is ground by that woman who will be taken; for "one will be taken," it says, "and the other left." The Church will be taken and the synagogue left; or the good mind will be taken and the wicked one abandoned. And so that you may know that Abraham too believed in Christ: "Abraham," he says, "saw my day and rejoiced." Whoever believes in Christ believes also in the Father, and whoever believes perfectly in the Father believes in the Son and the Holy Spirit. Three measures, then, but one fine flour; that is, there was one sacrifice, offered to the venerable Trinity with an equal measure of devotion, as it were, and a fitting fullness of piety.

Learn further about the zeal of prompt devotion. "He ran," it says, "and took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to his servant, and he hastened to prepare it." Everywhere his devotion is unflagging, and therefore his gift was acceptable to God. You also have it elsewhere that you should anticipate the sunrise with prayer: "Come," it says, "at the rising of the sun." You have in the Gospel the Lord Jesus saying: "Zacchaeus, make haste and come down." And he, who had obtained what he wanted — to see Christ — and had obtained still more — to be seen and called by Christ — came down in haste and received him joyfully. And therefore the Lord approved his affection and rewarded him with a swift recompense, saying: "Today salvation has come to this house." For the Lord too made haste to bestow his kindness, and so he did not wait to promise and then fulfill afterward, but acted first and declared it afterward. For he said, "Salvation has come," which is surely the word of one who acts first, not of one who promises. The just man, then, commends his vow by promptness. And therefore our fathers ate the passover in haste, with their loins girded, not taking off the fastenings of their sandals, and as though laying aside the burden of the body, so as to be ready for the crossing; for the Lord's passover is the passing from the passions to the exercise of virtue. And it is called the Lord's passover because then, in the figure of the lamb, the truth of the Lord's passion was proclaimed, and now its grace is celebrated.

So seek this quickly, my soul, so that you may also hear quickly, as Jacob heard: “What is this that you found so quickly, my son?” And he answered in keeping with sound doctrine: “That the Lord your God delivered it into my hands.” God gives quickly, for he spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were created. For the Word of God is not, as someone says, a work, but one who works, as you have it written: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” He goes before all things; for he is before all things, as the Father is, and in all things, as the same Father is, penetrating all things. For he is powerful and sharp, sharper than any sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and going before the thoughts of all. Of him God the Father says: “Now you will see whether my word overtakes you or not.” For where God is, there the Word is too, as he said: “We will come and make our dwelling with him.” And just as you have read elsewhere of God, “I stood here before you,” so the Word also says: “Before you stood under the fig tree, I saw you.” And of this same Word, that is, the Son of God, it was said: “Among you stands one whom you do not know.” For wherever the saints are, there in their midst is the Word of God, in the heart of each, filling seas and lands. And while he is here, he is also elsewhere, not by changing place but by filling every place with his presence; for he is everywhere who is through all things and in all things, leaving no place empty of himself; where he is present he already was, and where he was he is present. And so whoever knows that the Word of God is swift asks quickly and quickly obtains.

But Pharaoh, who spent his zeal on vain and empty notions, when Egypt was filled with frogs giving out an empty sound of things and a vain din, and Moses said to him, “Appoint me a time when I am to pray for you and for your servants and for your people, that the Lord may destroy the frogs,” though placed in such great necessity he ought to have asked him to pray at once and not delay, answered: “Tomorrow”—idle and careless, and about to pay the penalty for delay in the ruin of Egypt. And so, whenever he obtained what he asked, he became forgetful of the favor, and, puffed up in his fleshly mind, he forgot God.

It was humility, however, that commended prayer. Thus that Pharisee was rebuked, who counted up his fasts as if they were favors, as though he were throwing them in God's face, and declared himself free of sins; whereas the tax collector was praised, who, standing far off, would not lift his eyes to heaven but beat his breast, saying: “Lord God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” And so the divine verdict preferred him, saying that this tax collector went down justified rather than that Pharisee. For he is justified who confesses his own sin, as the Lord himself has said: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified.” And David says: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit,” and again: “A broken and humbled heart God does not despise.” Jeremiah too says: “A soul in distress and an anxious spirit cries out to you.” So both Pharaoh and the Assyrian, who said, “Which of the gods of these nations has delivered his land out of my hand, that your God should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?” were cast down by their own self-exaltation; but the righteous man, like Jacob, refers to God as their author whatever good things he has obtained, saying of everything he knows has prospered for him: “Because the Lord your God delivered them into my hands.” This, then, is the better way of paying vows, as David also says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High.” To praise God is to commend a vow and to pay it. That is why that Samaritan is preferred to the others: when he had been cleansed of leprosy along with nine other lepers, according to the Lord's command, he alone returned to Christ, magnified God and gave thanks. Of him Jesus said: “Was no one found among them to return and give thanks to God except this foreigner?” And he said to him: “Rise and go, for your faith has made you well.”

There is also this rule for commending prayer and vow: that we should not make our prayer public, but keep the mysteries hidden, as Abraham kept them, who made hearth cakes baked under the ashes. The fathers kept them too, who baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt, making unleavened cakes under the ashes, which in Greek are called enkryphiai [?] because they are hidden in the ashes. By this they signified—just as that leaven did which the woman in the Gospel hid in three measures until the whole was leavened—that the teaching of the mysteries too must be kept concealed. The Lord taught this more openly in his Gospel, saying: “But you, when you pray, go into your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you. And when you pray, do not speak much”; and further on: “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” Your room is the hidden place of your mind and the secret chamber of your soul. Go into this room of yours, that is, go deep within your heart; enter wholly, leaving the outer porch of your body, and shut your door.

Learn what your door is: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door around my lips.” And Paul asks that prayer be made for him, “that a door for the word may be opened to me,” he says, “to speak the mystery of Christ.” But he, chosen as he was to preach the Gospel, rightly wished a door for the word to be opened to him, since from his mouth came forth the salvation of the Gentiles, from his mouth issued the life of the nations. We, however, should shut the door, so that no fault may enter and no slip of speech go out. Fault enters if a slip goes out. Hear how fault enters: “In much talking,” it says, “you will not escape sin.” Much talking went out, sin came in, because in much talking the word that goes out is never weighed. It slips out without forethought, even though merely to say anything beyond measure is itself a great sin.

And so take care not to speak without forethought, for the lips of the imprudent lead him into evil. Take care not to exalt yourself in prayer, for the prayer of one who humbles himself has pierced the clouds. Take care not to divulge carelessly the mysteries of the Creed or of the Lord's Prayer. Or do you not know how grave it is to incur sin in prayer, where you hope for a remedy? Surely the Lord taught through the prophet that this is a heavy curse, saying: “And let his prayer become sin”—unless perhaps you think this a small matter. For to suppose that you will not be heard unless you shout is to distrust the power of God. Let your works cry out, let your faith cry out, let your love cry out, let your sufferings cry out, let your blood cry out, like that of holy Abel, of whom God said to Cain: “The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me.” He who cleanses in secret hears you in secret. We cannot hear anyone unless he speaks; but before God it is not words that speak but thoughts. And so that you may know this is true, the Lord Jesus said to the Jews: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” That is not the voice of one asking, but of one who knows. The evangelist makes this plain to you, saying: “But Jesus knew their thoughts.” As the Son knows, then, so the Father knows too. You have learned that the Son knows; to learn that the Father knows, hear the Father's counselor and witness saying: “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” So bake your hearth cake with the warmth of the Holy Spirit; bake also the passions of your soul with the heat of the Word. And if your passions are still rather raw, perhaps having only lately come out of Egypt, cover them and bake them through with gentle heat, lest they be unable to bear a stronger fire and be scorched rather than baked; for there are many things that displease when raw but delight when cooked. Cherish the deep mysteries in your breast, lest by untimely speech you entrust them, as it were half-baked, to faithless or weak ears, and the hearer turn away and loathe them with disgust.

Whereas, if he tasted them better baked, he would perceive the sweetness of spiritual food. In a divine way, moreover, the Lord Jesus taught you the goodness of the Father, who knows how to give good things, so that you may ask what is good from the One who is good; and he urged earnestly and often that we should pray—not that prayer should be drawn out tediously without a break, but that it should be frequent and constant. Empty things are often poured into a long prayer, while neglect creeps in altogether when prayer is broken off. Next he warns that when you ask pardon for yourself, you should know that it must above all be granted to others, so that you may commend your prayer by the voice of your deeds. The Apostle too teaches that we should pray without anger and dispute, so that your prayer is not disturbed or interrupted. He teaches also that we should pray in every place, although the Savior says: “Go into your room.” But understand this not as a room enclosed by walls, in which your limbs are shut in, but the room that is within you, in which your thoughts are enclosed and your senses move. This room of your prayer is with you everywhere and is secret everywhere, and it has no witness but God alone.

You are taught, moreover, to pray especially for the people as well, that is, for the whole body, for all the members of your mother, in which the mark of mutual love is seen. For if you ask for yourself, you will be asking for yourself alone; and if each prays only for himself, the grace of one who prays for himself is less than that of one who intercedes. But as it is, since each prays for all, all also pray for each. So, to conclude: if you ask only for yourself, you will, as we have said, be asking for yourself alone; but if you ask for all, all will ask for you, since you too are among all. So great is the reward that through the prayers of individuals each individual gains the support of the whole people. In this there is no arrogance, but greater humility and richer fruit.

But now it is time to move on to another point, since we have spoken fully about the fact that Cain made his offering after some days, which is a sign of lazy arrogance, since the very asking of a vow ought to be timely. Otherwise we may seem to have hoped for a remedy from human arts, that is, from medical skill and the juices of herbs, rather than to have asked help from God. For we must first take refuge in him who can cure the passions of our soul. But men, in a reversed order, first summon help for themselves from men, and only when human aid has failed do they think they must ask for the grace of divine favor.

With that point concluded, then, and Cain's offense proved, let us examine another fault in his offering. He offered from the fruits of the earth—not firstfruits to God from the first fruits. This amounts to claiming the firstfruits first for oneself and offering God what follows. So, since the soul is to be preferred to the body as a mistress to a servant, we ought surely to offer its firstfruits, that is, the firstfruits of the soul before those of the body. The firstfruits of the soul are the first movements toward good disciplines. Although these come later in time than the firstfruits of the body—which are food, growth, sight, hearing and touch, smell and voice (mind and sense, however, belong partly to the soul and partly to the body)—they are nevertheless first in the order of discipline. And the first of these is thanksgiving offered to God with a pure heart and simple speech.

These were the gifts Abel offered, and so God had regard for his gifts, because he offered from the firstlings. There is the further point that he offered of the firstlings of his sheep and of their fat. Notice that he offered not from things without sense but from living creatures. For what is animate is more than what is earthly, since the animate is nearest to the spiritual. For it is not the spiritual that comes first but the animate, and then the spiritual. What is animate breathes and has the breath of life; the same is not true of what comes from the fruits of the earth. Next, he offered not second things but first, not meager things but fat ones—such as the Law approved and commanded to be offered, as it is written: “And it shall be,” it says, “when God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to your fathers, and gives it to you, you shall set apart for the Lord every male that opens the womb. Every male that opens the womb among your herds and flocks, whatever is born to you, sanctify to the Lord. Every firstling of an ass you shall exchange for a sheep; and if you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it.” What could be of such profound mystery, of such deep and hidden wisdom, as this: that in certain veins of simple words you may detect and draw out the abundance of spiritual grace? For the Canaanites are fickle and restless. So when you have entered their land, and you see them driven from their possession because of their levity, restlessness and instability of character, hold fast to steadfastness yourself. Let no paltry reasoning, no frivolous talk unsettle you—for this is what the Canaanite is: shifting speech, unstable feeling and restless contention—but rather keep, in peace, tranquility of heart and serenity of mind, so that, as on the surge of the sea, you may provide a safe anchorage for ships in the harbor, as it were, of your mind.

This possession the Lord promises you, and he pledges it with the bond, as it were, of an oath, in order to strengthen your steadfastness. For God does not swear because he needs the trust of a believer, or because, lacking the support of witnesses, he requires the backing of an oath, as men do, who win trust for ourselves by an oath and swear precisely so that we may be believed to have spoken the truth. God, on the other hand, is faithful even when he simply speaks; his word is an oath. For God is not faithful on account of an oath; rather, the oath too is faithful on account of God. Why, then, does Moses represent God as swearing? Because we are shut in by a certain habit of mortals, and we wrap ourselves in common opinion as in a shell, like sea urchins, or like snails, which cannot breathe unless they are inside the covering of their shell, nor take in or endure the open air; so we move about only within certain earthly hiding places of human custom. Hence, since we usually believe more readily what is confirmed by an oath, God is written to swear so that our faith may not falter—God, who himself does not swear, but is the judge of those who swear and the avenger of those who perjure themselves. Thus it is written: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever.” He has certainly kept what he swore: he has given us an eternal High Priest, so that you too may know that what you swear must be kept, and that, since you swear by him who does not lie, you will find him your avenger if you lie.

So when restless and fickle thoughts have been driven out, God will give you the possession of your heart and mind cleared, so that you may cultivate it in tranquility and reap fruit from it; and you must not allow the Canaanites, that is, turbulent feelings, to return to it, but must root out the whole heathen enclosure of vices and tear down their groves, by which the truth is overshadowed and a certain free, heavenly vision of knowledge is hidden by the dread of murky dispute.

But you cannot accomplish this unless endowed with a divine gift. And so he says: “God will give you”—that is, the best thoughts, calm counsels, tranquil discoveries. When he has given these, you shall take every male that opens the womb and sanctify it to the Lord. God, who has given everything, does not demand everything from you. For he bestows many things for the use of human existence, and where there is natural use, there can be no divine sacrifice. Eating, drinking, sleeping and the other services of the body have been conferred on you as gifts; they are not gifts returned by you to God. But whatever holy thing you think, this is God's gift, God's inspiration, God's grace; just as, on the other hand, the things that belong to the use of human nature do not defile a man, but what comes out of the mouth—thefts, false witness, sacrileges—these are what defile a man.

Let us cleanse our inner selves, then, so that our offering may not displease. There let us seek every male that opens the womb, that is, what is just and foremost, which we ought to sanctify to the Lord. For it is not these bodily unions, conceptions and births, by which a woman's womb is opened once the modesty of her virginity is deflowered, that sanctify us. For although the wife may sanctify the husband and the husband the wife, yet it often happens that a virgin's womb is opened even without the holiness of marriage. Nor, again, does grace belong to the male alone while the woman is a stranger to sanctification; nor is the nature of the two sexes confused, so that both alike pour themselves out in bodily births. Men have their own tasks, and women have the distinct duties of their sex. This begetting for the succession of mankind befits the woman and is impossible for the man.

So if this meaning does not fit the use of the flesh, let us examine the functions of the soul. Here indeed I find something that is not divided by any sex. And though it has no sex, it performs the functions of both sexes: it marries, conceives and gives birth. And just as nature has given women a womb, in which the offspring of every living creature is formed over the course of months, so there is a certain power of the soul which, as in the hidden recess of a womb that generates, is accustomed to receive the seeds of our thoughts, to nurture what is conceived, and to bring forth births. For Isaiah would not otherwise have said, “We have conceived in the womb and brought forth the spirit of salvation,” unless he had known the womb of the soul. Of these offspring some are female: malice, wantonness, extravagance, intemperance, unchastity and other vices of this kind, by which a certain manliness of our soul is unnerved. Male are chastity, patience, prudence, temperance, fortitude and justice, by which our mind and the flesh itself are strengthened and roused to carry out the duties of virtue tirelessly. These are the offspring that prophetic womb brought forth. And so he says: “We have conceived in the womb and brought forth the spirit of salvation.” He, then, who poured forth the spirit of salvation both labored with and gave birth to a male.
Book Two

Let our soul be in labor with these offspring. Let it not only be in labor but also give birth, and give birth when its days are fulfilled, so that the day of judgment may not find its offspring unformed. For it was of such offspring that the Lord Jesus said: “Woe to those who are with child and to those who are nursing in those days.” So let this birth be completed early, and let our thoughts unfold in the progress of good works, so that our end may find nothing unfinished, the close of our life may come upon nothing left undone, and the course of our labor may leave nothing still lying, as it were, on the anvil. Make haste, then, my soul, to shape your offspring, to bring them to completion more quickly, and to nourish more speedily those you have brought forth.

The apostle shows the form of so great a birth when he says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” Let the whole inner being of our mind grow together into this form, and let Christ shine out in that life-giving womb of our soul. Let our offspring be faith, and let our nourishment be the precepts of doctrine. By these let the infancy of our heart, so to speak, be steeped, our childhood trained, our adolescence grow into youth, and our old age turn grey; for “an unblemished life is the true age of old age.” So that old age of the soul alone is good which no stains of faithlessness have defiled. And that is why Paul guards his offspring from this stain (“I begot you,” he says, “in the gospel”), so that no one's cruel whispering might tempt the infancy of their untried faith. He was therefore begetting males, he who longed that the peoples he taught should come together in the unity of the faith into a perfect man, and in the knowledge of the Son of God hold the perfect measure of the fullness of Christ. For he knew that this was the sacrifice acceptable to God, of which it is written: “Every male that opens the womb belongs to the Lord.” And since he added, “Everything that opens the womb, of your herds and of your flocks, the males belong to the Lord,” let us consider this, so that nothing in it remains obscure.

He had spoken of the chief offspring, that is, those that are full and capable of reason. He then added the offspring of the flock as well, that is, the rest of our senses, the common sort as it were, which are compared to irrational beasts of burden. Yet when these are governed by some ruler they are easily tamed. They grow used to carrying out orders and going under the yoke, and at their master's voice they quicken their pace, stop or turn aside, or perform whatever tasks of their work they are told to do, with something like human service. So strong is training that it overcomes nature. Thus creatures that do not share our substance still recognize the command of our voice. Though their own nature has no reason, they lay hold of the reason of our nature and in a way acquire it, as though it were poured into them. We see horses roused by the enthusiasm of the crowd, rejoicing in applause and delighted by their trainer's coaxing. We see fierce lions exchange their natural savagery for a gentleness that has been commanded, lay aside their fury and take on our ways; terrifying as they are, they learn to fear. A dog is beaten so that the lion may be afraid, and the beast that is enraged by injury to itself is held in check by injury to another and broken by another's example. How often, with prey at hand and food in front of them, they would rather go hungry, because they fear their trainer's displeasure! How often, driven by a sudden impulse, they open their jaws to bite and then release them at a command! So, while they obey our will, they forget their own. It is not so with wild beasts, or herds of horses, or any kind of livestock that roam without a ruler; deprived of all a tamer's guidance, they grow savage. That is why herdsmen, shepherds and other keepers have been appointed as masters of the flocks, so to speak, each shaping his duties to suit the condition of the animals entrusted to him.

It seems, then, that among our senses too one kind is tamed and gentle and another untamed. The untamed kind, when its herdsman, the movement of the mind, is idle and slack, as it were, rushes headlong after the irrational pleasures of the body. The gentle kind submits and subjects itself to the moderation of the mind as to a leader. Whatever is ruled by such a nature is masculine and perfect. But whatever holds sway without any leader, out of a kind of plebeian presumption, like a city deprived of the counsel of its king and nobles, makes the whole state of its body and its manly vigor effeminate with a womanish dissoluteness. To this kind belongs that law of the flesh which fought against the law of the apostle's mind and was dragging him captive by a certain law of sin. And so, to be freed from that body of death, Paul placed all his hope not in his own strength but in the grace of Christ. Hence it is clear that the movements that accord with the law of the mind proceed from divine favor, while the other impulses come from the will of the body.

The holy ones, then, are the firstborn of our senses; the others belong, as it were, to some flock and are of common, plebeian worth. Moses seems to have signified this to the Jews under various names. That mystical threshing floor of the law also makes it plain, of which he says: “You shall not make the first fruits of your threshing floor and of your wine press the last; you shall give me the firstborn of your sons.” The holy movements of our senses, those that accord with virtue, are themselves the first fruits of the spiritual threshing floor. That is why they are compared to the farm's threshing floor, where grain is winnowed. On the farm's threshing floor, wheat and barley are threshed and, by repeated winnowing, separated from the chaff: the chaff and other refuse of the harvest are scattered in all directions by the breath of a light breeze, while the more solid grain, once the dust is shaken off, falls back into the same place. In the same way, those of our thoughts that are solid and excellent provide a pure and genuine nourishment of virtue, as it is written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” But those that are useless and empty are scattered like smoke and mist, because “as smoke is to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who practice it.” And iniquity is rightly compared to smoke, for it clouds the sight of the mind like a sort of worldly fog.

And so the Lord says: “When you enter the land into which I am bringing you, and when you begin to eat of the bread of that land, you shall offer a separate offering to the Lord, a loaf as the first fruits of your dough. As with an offering from the threshing floor, so you shall set aside the first fruits of your mixtures and give them to the Lord.” We are a mixture, composed by a kind of mingling of different elements, since in us cold is mixed with hot and moist with dry. This dough holds many enticements of the flesh and a great many pleasures, but these are not the firstborn senses of this body. And since we consist of soul, body and spirit, this is the principal dough, in which the apostle desires us to be sanctified, as he says: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you in all things, and may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The first fruits of this dough are spiritual: they are the discoveries and offspring of the senses that proceed from the vigor of the soul. But not all senses are firstborn, only those that are free from malice, wickedness and every error. There are also necessary pleasures of the body, such as sleeping, eating, drinking, walking and other senses of this kind, but the first fruits are not among them. And so the Lord's sacred rite is not found in these but in those where there is chastity, piety, faith and devotion. A clear and evident example of this is the offering of the patriarch Isaac. His father offered him in the manner of a sacrifice, swayed by no movement of human passion, offering to God a pure victim, free of fear and untouched by bodily desire, for the father's very love for his son gave way to his devotion as he sacrificed.

Now let us consider what the force of first fruits is, and whether first fruits are reckoned by time or by holiness, that is, whether all firstborn things have the sanctity of first fruits. According to the law the first fruits of the crops are holy, because in them lies the best sacrifice of a prompt faith; but they become holy by devotion, not by time. It is not the yield that sanctifies but devotion. In fact, where the yield is early but devotion is slow, offense is incurred. So not all firstborn things are holy, but all holy things are also firstborn. Cain, for example, was firstborn, but not holy. Israel, too, is the holy people of God, but was not first in age; and yet he is called firstborn, as is written in the prophets: “Israel is my firstborn.” Levi also was holy but not firstborn, for we read that he was Leah's third son. And yet the Levites, whose name is derived from him, were called firstborn. For it is written in Numbers: “See, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine; for every firstborn is mine. On the day I struck down every firstborn of Egypt, I sanctified every firstborn of Israel.” So the Levites were called firstborn, since they were set above the other sons of Israel by their sanctification. Hear the apostle explain in what sense they are firstborn: “But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to ten thousands of rejoicing angels, and to the churches of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven.” He made four orders: Mount Zion, the city of Jerusalem, the festal throng of angels, and the churches of the firstborn. So the Lord God took the Levites from among the people of Israel, because he did not want them to share in human cares but to be ministers of divine worship. He made his firstborn those who open the spiritual womb; they were not firstborn from the womb of nature, like sinners guilty of various crimes, but are chosen once they have been stripped of worldly things. Hence they have no share in the possessions of the common people and are not counted in the midst of the people, because they possess the Word of God in their midst, as is written in the gospel: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,” and elsewhere: “In the midst of you stands one whom you do not know.”

From this, then, we learn that faith ought to commend us to God before all else. Once we have faith, let us strive to make our works perfect, since this is the full and perfect sacrifice, as the Lord himself teaches when he says of his gifts and offerings: “You shall take care to offer to me on my feast days, taking nothing away and dividing nothing, but offering what is full, whole and perfect.” The Lord's feast day is where the grace of perfect virtues is found. These virtues are perfect only if the mind, victorious over worldly anxieties and bodily enticement, shuts out the allurements of pleasure: free from the world, devoted to God, taking nothing away from the path of its straight purpose, and not dividing the seasons of its affection, now to luxury, now to labor. So only the wise man celebrates this feast, and no one else; for it is hard to find a soul free from passions of this kind. Divide the soul, then, according to reason into its ruling and its obedient parts, and then you will discover what is masculine and what is feminine; for there is no virtue without labor, since labor is the advance of virtue. The very words of the law also signify this, when it says: “Everything that opens the womb of a donkey you shall exchange for a sheep.” For the law separated unclean animals from sacrifice and ordered clean ones to be offered in their place. So it commands that the offspring of a donkey, which is unclean, be exchanged for a sheep, which is clean and fit for sacrifice. That is the literal meaning. But anyone who pursues the meaning of the spiritual law more deeply will reflect that the donkey is an animal of labor and the sheep an animal of fruit. He is saying, then, that labor must be exchanged for fruit, so that the end of one's work may be fruit. Or certainly in this sense: you shall commend all your labor and all your industry with a pure and simple disposition.

“But if you do not exchange it,” he says, “you shall redeem it.” Literally, then, the command is that another animal, or a price, be offered in place of the unclean animal, so that nothing inferior or unclean may seem to be offered among the tithes of the produce. But the deeper understanding teaches that your soul must be set free, so that it may turn away from things that bear no fruit; for whoever redeems himself frees himself and sheds a kind of debt. We must abandon works that cannot have true fruit and good progress, such as these worldly ones, whose use cannot last. In them the achievement itself proves bare and empty of truth, and though it was sought with the greatest labor, it does the soul no good. For everything that brings servitude upon the soul is useless, even if it does not lack success.
