Great seems the victory of those who fight and the glory of those who triumph; yet we often see the very men who have conquered fall again under the uncertainties of war, pass into the enemy's hands through the outcome of a battle, and become all the more wretched for having once been victors. You must therefore direct your works to God and let his favor breathe upon you. The athlete, who contends with his own strength and not another's, believes every time he enters the contest that he faces an uncertain outcome; and when he has won the crown, he realizes that this worldly glory withers faster than the leaves of the crown itself. The helmsman, when he has brought his ship into harbor, scarcely thinks his labor has come to an end, and at once looks for labor to begin again. The soul is released from the body, and even after the end of this life it is held in suspense by the uncertainty of the judgment to come. So there is no end where an end is supposed to be. Therefore let us cling to our God with prayers, a pure conscience and a spirit of love, and win the divine favor for ourselves, praying that we may be released and set free from worldly cares as from harsh and boorish masters, and may go out from the world's servitude, called into the freedom of heavenly knowledge, which is the true and only freedom.

And to support the precept of the law with an example: when the Egyptians oppressed the Jewish people with various works, with clay and stone, the children of Israel groaned and called down the Lord's mercy upon themselves. And he said to Moses: “I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel, how the Egyptians oppress them in slavery, and I have remembered my covenant. Go and say to the children of Israel: I am the Lord. I will bring you out from the power of the Egyptians and rescue you from their slavery, and I will set you free with an uplifted arm and with great judgment. I will take you to myself as a people and will be your God, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who will bring you out from the power of the Egyptians and bring you into the land over which I stretched out my hand.” See how the Hebrew people exchanged labor for fruit, so that those who toiled in clay came to work for the hope of an eternal kingdom. So too the Lord in the gospel took pity on the empty labor of the Gentile peoples, who made bricks for a muddy superstition and, given over to bodily pleasure, could not build the solid wall of faith; and speaking as if to the offspring of a donkey, he said: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” In this call I seem to recognize more fully the words and mysteries of the law, which taught that the donkey must either be exchanged for a sheep or redeemed with money, so that we not only exchange the offspring of the donkey for a sheep, that is, the unclean for the clean, but also redeem it. This seems to express the following: if we first wash away the stains of our sins through the sacrifice of purification and the mystery of baptism, we should also redeem our crimes by good works, by the price of faith, and by mercy.

Our price is the blood of Christ. So the apostle Peter says: “You were redeemed not with gold or silver, but with precious blood.” And Paul says: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men.” So it is not without reason that people in the gospel marvel that the Lord Jesus sat on the colt of a donkey, for the Gentile people, which according to the law was held unclean, began to be Christ's offering. It is also written of the Levites that they are the redemption of the others, because by the holiness of their life and by prayer they would lighten the sins of the people. In them the figure of the lamb foreshadowed in mysteries the true Levite who was to come, who by the suffering of his own body would take away the sin of the world. “Levite” means “taken up for me” or “he is light for me.” He bears the sign of perfect virtue and of the health to be imparted to the people. He it is, then, who came, awaited for the salvation of all: for me he was born of a virgin's womb, for me he was offered, for me he tasted death, for me he rose again. In him the redemption of all men was taken up and resurrection assumed. He is the true Levite, so that he might make us Levites: that we might cling to God, pour out continual prayers to him, hope for salvation from him, flee earthly business, and be numbered among God's possession, as it is written: “O Lord, possess us.” For that is the only possession which, exposed to no storms, bears the fruits of everlasting grace. The Levite is a redeemer, because a wise man is the redemption of a fool. Like a physician he tends the fool's sick mind and sprinkles remedies of prudence on it to make it sounder, imitating that Physician who came from heaven to show men the ways of prudence and to reveal the paths of wisdom to little ones. He saw that those who were suffering could not be saved without a remedy, and so he gave medicine to the sick; he brought the help of health to all, so that whoever perishes may ascribe the causes of his death to himself, since he refused to be cured even though he had a remedy by which he could escape. Thus the mercy of Christ toward all may be openly proclaimed, for those who perish perish by their own neglect, while those who are saved are set free in accordance with the will of Christ, who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Indeed, if Sodom had had fifty righteous men, it would not have been overthrown, and if it had had ten, it would have been redeemed; for the word of the forgiveness of sins strips the soul of its servitude, and the fullness of perfect discipline does not allow the mind to be consumed by the devouring heat of lust.

Yet it matters greatly, and builds up our moral disposition, if we also take the number of the righteous in its simple sense, as something that benefits the salvation of peoples. It checks and cuts away envy, confounds wickedness, spurs on virtue and increases grace. For no one ought to envy another a praise that benefits himself; and a wicked man, when he accepts his redeemer, often imitates him, certainly reveres him, and frequently even loves him. And the righteous man himself, if he knows that he will benefit others, grows in zeal, and by that grace binds peoples together and heaps up the love of citizens and the glory of cities. How blessed is the city that has many righteous men! How celebrated it is on everyone's lips, how blessed on every side, and how happy and lasting its condition is thought to be! How I rejoice when I see gentle and wise men living long, when I behold chaste virgins and grave widows of great age, like a [?] grey-haired senate of the Church, which by its very countenance and grave bearing displays something to revere, something to imitate, something by which to be colored with every grace of character! I do not rejoice for their own sake, since many wearinesses of this world come upon one who lives long, but because they benefit many. Likewise, when one of these falls, even if laid to rest after a long old age, I am grieved, because the flock of the young is deprived of the wall of the old. Indeed, this is the first sign of a city about to perish, or of impending evils or coming ruin: when its wiser men or even its graver women pass away. It is here that the gate is first opened to the evils that rush in. Just as a whole city is strengthened and enlarged by an assembly of the wise, or shaken by their death, so grave speech, a kind of aged speech full of prudence, tends to steady each person's soul and confirm the mind. And if there is added the practice of much reading, a kind of senate of many precepts and counsels, it brings even a lasting stability to that city which is in each person's heart.

This, then, is why Moses called the Levites firstborn and redeemers of the rest: because men of riper and useful judgment, in the one respect, display a kind of old age of the soul and, in the other, confer redemption. Hence also in the Old Testament Moses designated the cities of the Levites as cities of redemption, because whoever flees to that soul in which the Word of God dwells, which is fortified and walled like a city, gains perpetual freedom for himself. In the cities of the Levites there was remission of penalties: if someone who had caused a man's death unintentionally fled to them, no one was permitted to kill him as long as he remained within the cities of the Levites. In the same way, whoever repents of a sin of his own that he committed unwittingly or unwillingly, if he clings to residence among the Levites and does not think of leaving these teachers who dispense the commandments of God, is freed by the law itself from all punishment and penalty for the crime he committed.

Do not think it absurd that criminals dwell with the devout and the stained with the consecrated; for those who have been polluted by some contagion of sin need to be purified. And in a way the two cases converge from different directions. As the Levite, having renounced worldly pleasures, is an exile from guilt, so the man guilty of bloodshed is a fugitive from his homeland. But there is this difference: the latter leaves his own people out of necessity, for fear of the law, whereas the minister of God renounces fellowship with human passions and disowns a kind of kinship with carnal enticement for the sake of pursuing virtue. This too is not far from the truth, that he also, as it were, lays hands on himself, to kill the pleasures of his body and bring about a kind of death of his flesh. Moses did indeed kill the Egyptian and became a fugitive from the land of Egypt, to escape the tyrant of that land. But he would not have killed that Egyptian man had he not first slain within himself the Egyptian of spiritual wickedness and renounced the luxury of royal honors, esteeming the reproach of Christ a greater inheritance than the treasures of Egypt. To fools this seems a reproach, but to us that reproach of the Lord's cross is the power and wisdom of God.

There is also the fact that God has two principal kinds of power: one by which he forgives, the other by which he punishes. Sins are forgiven through the Word of God, whose interpreter and, in a sense, executor the Levite is; they are forgiven through the office of the priest and the sacred ministry. They are also punished through men, such as judges, who hold power for a time, as the apostle teaches when he says: “Would you be free from fear of authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it; for it is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for it does not bear the sword for nothing. It is God’s minister, an avenger to bring wrath on the one who has done evil.” Sins are punished through nations as well, as we read, for the Jewish people were often subdued by foreigners whom God stirred up at his command because they had offended the divine majesty. Not even the man who has unwillingly committed a homicide stands outside this ministry, since the law says of him that God delivered the other into his hands. His hands, then, served divine vengeance as an instrument does. So the Levite is the minister of forgiveness, while the slayer, who committed homicide not by design but against his will, is the minister of divine vengeance. Note this too: when the ungodly man is slain, Christ is poured in, and where abomination is done away with, holiness is gathered in. For the Lord said:

“On the day on which I slay every firstborn of Egypt, I will sanctify to myself every firstborn of Israel.” You should apply this not to a single day of Egypt’s affliction but to all time. For when wickedness is renounced, virtue is taken up at once: the exit of malice brings about the entrance of virtue, and the same effort that shuts out crime joins innocence to us. You have this in the Gospel. When Satan thrust himself into the heart of Judas, Christ withdrew from him, and in the very moment that Judas received the one, he lost the other. So it is written: “And after the morsel, Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to him: What you are doing, do quickly.” What does this mean? That since Satan had entered him, he should go away from Christ. So he is cast out and thrust away, because one who had begun to be with the devil could no longer be with the Lord Jesus; for Christ has no fellowship with Belial. That is why, driven out by the command, he left at once, as we read in the evangelist’s words: “When he had taken the morsel, he went out immediately; and it was night.” He not only went out, but went out immediately, and at night. Small wonder that one who was deserting Christ had the darkness of night about him. But just as Judas, received by the devil, was shut out by Christ, so Zacchaeus, renouncing greed, received Christ. And rightly, seeing his eagerness in climbing a tree to see Jesus as he passed by, the Lord says: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” And he came down in haste and welcomed him joyfully. But in welcoming Christ he shut out greed, banished faithlessness, and renounced fraud; for Christ does not enter except to shut out vices, since he does not dwell with errors. Indeed, he drove the moneychangers out of the temple because he himself wished to dwell there. So Zacchaeus, understanding that he could not receive Christ with his old disposition, ordered his former vices to leave his house so that Christ might enter. Rightly, then, when people grumbled that the Lord Jesus had gone to stay with a sinful man, he said to the Lord: “Look, half of my goods I give to the poor, and if I have taken anything from anyone by fraud, I repay it fourfold.” In this he answered those who said that a sinner ought not to have offered Christ hospitality, as if to say: “I am no longer a tax collector, no longer that Zacchaeus, no longer a robber or a cheat. I give back what I took; I give back, I who used to take away. Now I give to the poor whom I once stripped bare; now I bestow my own goods, I who used to seize the goods of others.” Crimes fled once Christ entered; all the blindness of the fleshly passions was dispelled when the light of eternal life was poured in.

We have spoken of the firstborn; let us speak also of the fat portions. David teaches enough about these when he says: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness.” And earlier he says: “And may your burnt offering be made fat,” teaching that the acceptable sacrifice is the one that is rich and sleek, fattened on the fodder of faith and devotion and on the more abundant nourishment of the heavenly word. We often call a work “fat” when we want it understood as dense and laborious, and a victim is called “choice” when it is not thin and meager. So we rightly call a sacrifice “fat” when we wish to declare it choice. A further proof is that in the prophetic interpretation the fat cows were likened to fruitful years.

Now let us consider what the Lord means when he says: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still.” This shows that God is not appeased by the gifts offered, but by the disposition of the one offering them. Thus Cain, offerer of a condemned gift, understood from his awareness that his offering was insincere that his sacrifice had not been approved by God, and he became sad. For when the mind is conscious of having done right, it rejoices, and the soul is filled with joy as though by a spiritual infusion when one’s efforts or works are not disapproved by God. Cain’s sadness, then, was the witness of his conscience and the sign of his rejection. And although he offered a gift, he fell into guilt because he did not divide it rightly and properly.

For there were four ways in which sacrifices were made acceptable: if they were “new of the new,” or roasted, or divided, or continual. The “new of the new” were offered at the beginning of the year and were reckoned in figure among the firstfruits; but now it has been revealed that they signify those who are renewed through the sacraments of baptism. For this is truly the sacrifice of firstfruits: when each person offers himself as a victim and begins with himself, so that afterward he can offer his gift. So the new faith of the renewed is fit for sacrifice: strong, youthful, growing in virtue, not slack or weary, not withered by old age or sluggish in vigor. It should sprout with a green shoot of wisdom and grow up in the youthful fervor of divine knowledge, yet it should still have the sap of the old teaching. For the teaching of the Old Testament ought to go together with that of the New, since it is written: “Eat the old of the old, and clear away the old before the new.” Let the knowledge of the patriarchs be our food; let the mind feast on the oracles in the books of the prophets. Let the inner mind be fed on such fattening fare, but now let it be not the figure of the lamb but the reality of Christ’s body. Let not the shadow of the law dazzle our eyes; rather, let the grace of the Lord’s passion and the splendor of the resurrection openly enlighten the eye of the mind.

“If you offer a sacrifice from the firstling sheep, roasted in fire, roasted and rich, you will offer a sacrifice of firstfruits,” as it is written. This means that your faith ought to be tested as if by fire and to burn with the Holy Spirit. Thus Jacob cooked lentils and snatched from his brother the primacy of the blessing, which a solid faith would surely obtain. So the one grew stronger and more vigorous, while the other, who did not know how to cook his own food, grew faint and failing and wasted away. Let the strength of your soul, then, be burned by the word of the Lord as by fire. See how Joseph was burned, as it is written: “The word of the Lord burned him.” Let your faith be parched like ears of grain at harvest; for they show their fruit to be ripe when the summer season has parched them at the sun’s first advance. So the abundant word of the Scriptures strengthens the soul and colors it with the warmth of spiritual grace; it also strengthens what reason has found and breaks the whole force of the irrational passions. That is why Esau went slack, the bonds of his strength loosened, while those who were commanded, with loins girded, to eat the head of the lamb not raw nor boiled in water but roasted in fire, as you have in Exodus, crossed the sea on foot with strong and faithful hearts. In the Gospel too, the Lord Jesus, in whom the fullness of the Holy Spirit overflowed, ate roasted fish, as it is written. And perhaps Esau failed for this reason: he craved food boiled in water, which Jacob gave to him in his weakness as something unsuited to himself.

Offering and prayer, then, ought not to be confused but distinguished by a fitting division. In every confusion distinction is better, and much more so in prayer and offering, which become obscure unless they have definite divisions. That is why the law commonly commands the victim’s limbs to be divided and burnt offerings to be presented, so that the sacrifice may be unmixed, uncovered and bare; for our faith ought to burn bare and stripped of every wrapping, not clothed in wandering and deceitful opinions, so that the pure and sincere simplicity of the mind may appear. Then let it be divided into its proper parts. For virtue is a genus divided into many species, but the principal ones are four: prudence, temperance, fortitude and justice. Let your prayer, then, breathe prudence regarding the knowledge of God and the truth of the faith. Let it breathe temperance, which the apostle thought should be required even of married couples when he said: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” And the law commands those who have kept themselves chaste since the day before and the day before that to come to the sacrifice. Let prayer hold fast to fortitude, so that no fear interrupts it and no weariness makes it fail; for our intent in praying ought to be strongest when we are pressed by adversity. Let prayer guard justice; had Judas kept it, his prayer would not have become sin. For when ought we to abstain more from unjust deeds and pursuits than when we pray for God’s justice? And so the Lord, so that justice might be dear to our hearts, said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” This was lacking in Judas; had it been present, he would not have betrayed the Lord or handed over his master. It was lacking also in the sacrifice of this Cain, who, had he held to justice, ought to have brought the Lord the first gifts, not the later ones. And so he lacked division, and therefore the answer says: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still.” You see how great a fault this is: where division is lacking, the whole sacrifice is rejected.

It remains for us to speak of continual and unceasing prayer, for we ought to persevere and give ourselves to prayer. The Lord spent whole nights in prayer, not for his own benefit but to teach us. Frequent prayer produces a kind of discipline in praying, since practice itself makes people teachable by God, while neglect makes them unteachable. Exercise, then, is good. The body’s strength is increased by frequent exercise, but without exercise it dwindles and declines; indeed, many have lost even their natural strength through falling out of the habit of exercise. In the same way the soul’s fortitude is made firm by constant exercise, so that the labor of discipline becomes not a burden but a benefit. Let us bring our minds this food, which, ground and refined by much meditation, may strengthen the heart of man like that heavenly manna. Not without reason were we told that the manna was ground and refined: we must long grind and refine the words of the heavenly Scriptures, turning them over with all our mind and heart, so that the sap of that spiritual food may spread through all the veins of the soul. If, then, faith grows up as though in youth, casting off the weakness of a devotion grown old; if it burns with the Spirit; if it is held by fitting distinction to the measure of lawful division; and if perseverance commends its grace, then there comes about that rich and, as it were, fat kind of prayer of which the prophet says: “You have made my head rich with oil.” For as lambs grow fat on plentiful milk and well-pastured sheep glisten with fat, so the prayer of the faithful grows rich when it feeds on the apostolic sap.

If any of the things we have mentioned above is lacking, the sacrifice is not approved. That is why it was said to Cain: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly...” For we read that the world itself was made with distinction, though before part of it was unordered, since “the earth was invisible and unformed.” Light was made first, and God called the light, and God separated the light from the darkness, and the darkness was called night. And we read that each thing was made in order: heaven, earth, fruit-bearing trees, various animals. The lighter elements, such as air and fire, were assigned to the higher places, and the heavier, that is water and earth, to the lower. God could certainly have ordered all things to be made at once, but he preferred to keep a distinction, so that we might imitate it in all our affairs, and above all in returning favors. In these it is not enough to give back what you have received; you must also make what you give back commendable. For if someone pays a debt and insults his creditor in repaying it, that is surely more intolerable than not having repaid what he owed. So what is considered is not the amount paid but the spirit, the manner and the disposition of the one repaying. Cain offered rightly, then, since an offering is a mark of devotion and a sign of gratitude, but he did not divide rightly, since he ought first of all to have brought God the firstfruits, so as to begin with thanks to the Author. For this is the order of division: what is first should come before what is second, not the second before the first, and heavenly things should be preferred to earthly, not earthly to heavenly.

But because Cain confused this order, he is told: “You have sinned; be still.” God teaches us everything: first, not to sin, as he warned in Adam’s case; second, if you have sinned, to be still, as you are taught in Cain’s case. For we ought to blush at sin and condemn it, not defend it, since guilt is lessened by shame and heaped up by defense; by keeping silent we are corrected, by arguing we fall. Let there at least be modesty where there is no acquittal. Hence the saying: “The just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech.” And again we read elsewhere that the Lord himself said: “Tell your iniquities, that you may be justified.” How great is the grace of shame, that modesty should keep the justice that the guilt of sin had taken away! He says “be still,” then, because you have nothing to plead in excuse. “Its turning is back to you.” For it is not his brother who is charged with it; rather, the error is ascribed to him of which he is himself the author. The crime that began with you, he says, comes back to you. You have no grounds for blaming necessity rather than your own mind.

Your wickedness is turned back on you; you are its chief. He puts it well: “You are its chief.” For ungodliness is a kind of mother of offenses, and one who has committed graver sins easily slides into the rest. How can a man who has violated divine things restrain himself in human ones, or be good to men when he has wronged God? The other vices follow the more atrocious guilt of crime, because others lean the way that wickedness has tilted. You, then, are the chief of your own deed, the ringleader of the crime. No error drew you in against your will or unawares; you were guilty by choice, by deliberate judgment, and you did not commit treachery through a slip. By this you yourself prove yourself guilty of an offense against God.

So, warned to be still, he grows more insolent and makes his crime worse. What does he mean when he says, “Let us go into the field,” unless that a place bare of growing things is chosen for the killing of a kinsman? Where was the brother to be slain but where fruit was lacking? As though foreseeing so great a crime, nature had denied that place any growth, for it was not fitting that the same soil should receive, against nature, the defilement of a kinsman’s blood and also, according to nature, bring forth fruit. Rightly he himself says, “Let us go into the field”; he does not say, “Let us go into paradise,” where fruit trees blossom, nor into any cultivated and fruitful place. Those who kill their kin show for themselves that they can have no fruit from their crime, and that fruit does not remain with those who have lent their service to so great an impiety. For they shun the very kindness of the elements, like this Cain, who seems to have feared that a more generous yield of good things from the earth might hinder his grim deed, and that the earth, by its habitual generosity in giving birth, by which it makes its varied offspring and fruits sprout, might, even amid these preparations for the crime, recall him to brotherly affection by its mere silent appearance. The robber shuns daylight as a witness to his crime, the adulterer shuns light as though blushing before an accomplice, the killer of kin shuns the fertility of the earth. For how could one bear to see the fellowship of the common offspring of the earth when he was butchering the partner of his own blood? Joseph is thrown into a dry pit; Amnon is slain inside a house. So nature passed a just judgment by depriving the places where kin would be slain of the dowry of her bounty, so that by a kind of condemnation of the innocent soil she might show how great the punishments of the guilty would be. Because of men’s crimes, then, even the elements themselves are condemned. Thus David wished the punishment of perpetual barrenness on the mountains where Jonathan was slain with his father, saying: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall on you, mountains of death!”

Now let us consider why God asked Cain where his brother was, as though he did not know he had been killed. As far as God’s knowledge is concerned, he refutes Cain’s denial, and when Cain disowns the deed, he replies as one who knows: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me.” But as far as the deeper reason is concerned, he is urging sinners to repentance, for confession cuts punishment short. That is why in worldly courts those who deny are placed on the rack and tortured, while the judge is moved by a certain pity for one who confesses. There is a kind of modesty in sins, and it is part of repentance to admit the crime and not shift the blame but acknowledge it. The shame of the accused softens the judge, while the stubbornness of those who deny provokes him. God wants to call you to seek pardon; he wants indulgence to be hoped for from him; he wants your confession to show that he is not the author of wickedness. For those who attribute their sin to some [?], as the pagans claim, seem to blame the divine powers for the necessity of their decree or their working, as though the force of those powers were the cause of sin; for one who kills under some compulsion kills, as it were, against his will. What comes from us has no excuse, while what lies outside us can be excused. But how much graver than the sin itself it is to attribute what you have done to God, and to shift the odium of your guilt onto the author not of crime but of innocence!

Now weigh the killer’s answer: “I do not know,” he says; “am I my brother’s keeper?” Though these words betray defiance, they nonetheless imply that, had he thought well of his brother, he ought to have been the keeper of family love. For whom ought he to have protected more than his brother? But how could he keep the duty of brotherhood when he did not acknowledge the affection of kinship? Or how could one who showed no reverence to God pay obedience to nature? First he denies, as though before someone ignorant; he refuses the duty of keeping his brother, as though he had no share in nature; he evades the judge, as though answerable to no one. Why are you surprised that he did not acknowledge family love when he did not acknowledge his Maker? And so this sequence of the Scriptures teaches you that faith is the root of all the virtues. That is why the apostle says that our foundation is Christ, and that only what you build on this foundation will profit you toward the fruit of your work and the reward of virtue.

Fittingly, then, the Lord answered him who denied so foolishly, saying: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me.” That is: “Why do you not know where your brother is? You two were alone with your two parents; among so few, your brother could not have escaped your notice. Or is it because your parents cannot be your accusers? For I do not want the kinship that is the author of safety to become the author of danger, as though in you alone nature had lost its laws. Do you think the crime is hidden, then, because parents ought not to accuse? But that makes your condemnation all the greater. For if the dear names of kinship ought not to accuse, much less ought they to kill. But if you reject me as witness and shun me as judge, the voice of your brother’s blood, which cries out to me, is the witness. It convicts you with greater authority than if your brother were alive. You were alone: who else could have killed him? If you accuse your parents, you prove yourself a parricide. One who does not spare his parents could kill his brother; one who wants to prove himself born of parricides could be a parricide. And he puts it well: the voice of the blood cries out, not the brother cries out. That is, even in death he keeps his innocence and the grace of brotherhood: the brother does not accuse, lest he seem a killer of his kin; neither his voice nor his soul accuses, but the voice of the blood which you yourself shed. So it is your own deed that accuses you, not your brother.” At the same time the criminal is deprived of any grounds for complaint. One who confesses the crime by his own deed cannot complain about another’s testimony. Words are less than the deed. Yet the earth too is a witness, for it received the blood.

And he puts it well: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out from the earth.” He did not say, “It cries out from your brother’s body,” but, “It cries out from the earth.” Even if your brother spares you, the earth does not spare you; if your brother is silent, the earth condemns you. It is both witness and judge against you: a sharper witness, since it is still wet with the blood of your kinsman whom you killed; a harsher judge, since it was polluted by so great a crime that it opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. It had indeed opened its mouth as though to receive words of affection from the brothers, fearing nothing when it saw brothers, for it knew that the bond of brotherhood is an incentive to love, not to hatred. How could it suspect the murder of a brother when it had not yet seen any killing? “But you shed blood, and grieving over its defilement,” he says, “the earth will no longer yield its strength to you.” How innocent a vengeance, that the earth, so grievously violated, is content not to benefit you and does not seek to harm you!

There is also no small teaching in his words, "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me," for God hears his righteous ones even when they are dead, since they live to God. They are rightly counted among the living: though they have tasted the death of the body, they still enjoy a bodiless life, are lit by the splendour of their own merits, and delight in eternal light as well. So he hears even the blood of the righteous, but he turns away from the prayers of the wicked. Even if the wicked seem to be alive, they are more wretched than all the dead, for they carry their flesh about like a tomb in which they have buried their unhappy soul. What else is a soul but buried when it rolls about in the dirt and is shut in by the desires of earthly greed and the other vices, so that it cannot breathe the breeze of heavenly grace? A sinner of this kind is cursed from the earth, which is the lowest and last part of the world. Higher, surely, are heaven and the things in heaven: sun, moon and stars, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, cherubim and seraphim. There is no doubt, then, that the higher things have condemned the one whom the lower things condemned. How could he be acquitted by the pure, heavenly verdict above when not even the earth could acquit him? And so he is ordered to be groaning and trembling upon the earth.

The reason is plain and holds generally: every wicked person has evils both present and to come. Present evils produce sadness and future ones fear, but the wicked are troubled more by what is present than by what is to come. That is why Cain said to the Lord: "My case is too great. If you abandon me today, I will hide myself from your face." For nothing is more grievous for one who has gone astray than to be deserted by God, so that he cannot bring himself back. The death of a sinner puts an end to his sinning, but a life deprived of God's guiding hand plunges headlong and slides into worse things. When a shepherd leaves his flock, wild beasts attack; in the same way, when God deserts a man, the devil rushes in. It is especially grievous for the foolish to have no one to steer them. Where medicine is lacking, wickedness spreads and the wound grows worse. And the one who wants to veil his fault and cover his sin hides himself. For whoever does evil hates the light and seeks darkness as a hiding place for his offences. The righteous man, however, does not usually hide from the Lord his God. Instead he presents himself, saying:

"Here I am." He says this because he has no guilty conscience that he fears will be found out. It is fitting, then, that the man with a bad conscience hides and says: "Whoever finds me will kill me." A narrow-minded man fears the death at hand and ignores the everlasting one. He has no dread of God's judgment and begs only to be spared the destruction of his body. But by whom did he fear being killed, when he had no one on earth but his parents? He could indeed fear attacks from wild beasts. Having violated the rights of the divine law and taught that a human being could be killed, he could not count on the other animals staying subject to him. He could also fear that his parents would become murderers of their own kin, since he had taught that kin-murder could be committed. His parents too could learn from their son what later generations learned from a parent.

Now let us consider why God said, "Whoever kills Cain will suffer vengeance sevenfold," and why a sign is placed on him so that the murderer is not killed, when no such provision had been made to keep the innocent man from being killed. A human being is an eighth thing. He has reason, by which he excels the other creatures; he has the five senses of the body; he has a voice; and he has the gift of begetting. Unless these seven are ruled by the faculty of reason, they are subject to death, and so the fool's whole danger lies in them. Whoever has lost that faculty of reason will flatter himself in vain that he can use these seven gifts of the flesh. They all fall apart unless they are held in check by the reins of reason. So the death of reason brings about the death of the irrational passions. But a better explanation is that seven is the number of rest and forgiveness. Whoever does not spare another sinner and begrudges him the gift of forgiveness of sins will rob himself of the hope of forgiveness. The vengeance he suffers will match the grace he refused.

When God placed a sign on Cain so that no one would kill him, he wanted to turn the wanderer back and invite him to amend his life through this kindness, since we usually entrust ourselves more readily to those we are indebted to. Yet God does not grant him much. In that very act he punishes the fool's folly: though Cain was liable to everlasting punishment, he did not ask for his penalty to be remitted but thought he should plead for the life of this body, which holds more hardship than pleasure. There is only one death, consisting in the separation of soul and body and the end of this life, and when it comes it ordinarily takes away all the body's pains rather than adding to them. But the fears that so often assail people while they live this life, together with sorrows, pains, groans, various torments, and the wounds of hardship and illness, inflict a great many deaths on the human race. This death therefore seems a remedy rather than a punishment. It does not destroy, for it does not take life away but moves it on to better things. Even when the guilty die, having refused to draw back from their sins, they reach an end, even against their will, and it is the end of their guilt, not of their nature. They are kept from committing further offences, since for them life only accumulates interest on their sins.

But if they have a good hope, we should believe that they move on rather than perish. At this point the teaching on the incorruptibility of the soul is introduced. The true and blessed life is the one that each person with a good conscience lives far more purely and blessedly once our soul has laid aside the wrapping of this flesh and been released from what is, as it were, the prison of the body. Then it flies back to that higher place from which it was poured into our inmost being. There it groaned in sympathy with this body until it had fulfilled the office of governing entrusted to it, which was to guide and restrain the irrational impulses of this flesh by the rule of reason. This is why the prophets later went into captivity with the Jewish people. They did not want the remnant of the holy people to be left without protection or counsel and so suffer greater hardship. Instead, warned by the prophets' frequent oracles, the people would turn back to the Lord their God with devoted hearts. They would not be so worn down by the misfortunes of captivity that they fell headlong into the sin of faithlessness and despaired of the remedy of eternal salvation.

So this passage refutes those who think that the only life is the one in this world, where everything is full of falling and full of grief, and they are refuted simply by the course of events. Look: the righteous, innocent and devout man incurred his brother's hatred because of the favour his devotion won him, and he was carried off by murder while still young. Yet the wicked, criminal and impious man, polluted even with his brother's blood, lived a long life, took a wife, left descendants and founded cities, and he obtained this by God's permission. Does not the voice of God cry out plainly in these things? You are wrong if you think that all the good of living is found here. Do you not understand, do you not notice, that this old age is a veteran of miseries and that advancing years are the wages paid for hardships? Like Scylla we are surrounded by the roar of daily shipwrecks, battered by the waves and living in rocky dens, and we take delight in them as that creature did, which was not so much eternal as an immortal evil. So the long life granted to this Cain was also a punishment, because he lived in fear and ran a long course with much fruitless labour. No punishment is more grievous than to be the cause of greater punishments for oneself. See, then, how everlasting is the life of the righteous and how the life of the wicked amounts to nothing. The blood of the righteous man cries out even though he is dead, but the life of the sinner is hidden.

The third point is this. Kin-murder had been committed, which is the chief of crimes. As soon as sin crept in, the law of divine clemency had to be extended at once. Otherwise, if the guilty man had been punished immediately, people too might show no patience or moderation when they judged and might hand the accused over to punishment straight away. God's providence in this sentence was meant to teach judges magnanimity and patience. No one should be swept away too hastily by zeal for vengeance and, through rash and hurried deliberation, punish the innocent or make harsher the penalty of the ungrateful. Yet God did not allow a full pardon for one who had shown no repentance for his crime. He drove Cain from his presence, and Cain, disowned by his parents, was banished to a kind of exile in a separate dwelling, because he had passed from human gentleness to the savagery of beasts. Even so, God did not want the murderer to be punished by murder, for he would rather a sinner be corrected than die. This is why vengeance is taken on Lamech seventy-seven times: the guilt of one who did not correct himself even after another had been condemned is heavier. Cain had sinned earlier from a thoughtless impulse, but Lamech certainly ought to have guarded against what he had seen condemned in another. The sentence was reserved for its proper judge, so that no one would think the accused could be struck down by anyone at all. And to come to the mystery: he ought not to have killed one who had time to repent until the natural end of his death. Cain could have pleaded that he would have redeemed himself, even by a late act of repentance, had a premature punishment not snatched him away.
